claim: AACs (axo-axonic cells) are also called chandelier cells (ChCs) in the cerebral cortex.
source: Axo-axonic cells (AACs), also called chandelier cells (ChCs) in the cerebral cortex, are the most distinctive type of GABAergic interneurons described in the neocortex, hippocampus, and basolateral amygdala (BLA).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established naming convention.

claim: AACs selectively innervate glutamatergic projection neurons (PNs) at their axon initial segment (AIS).
source: AACs selectively innervate glutamatergic projection neurons (PNs) at their axon initial segment (AIS), thus may exert decisive control over PN spiking and regulate PN functional ensembles.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of AACs stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: AACs are deployed across essentially all the pallium-derived brain structures.
source: We discovered that AACs are deployed across essentially all the pallium-derived brain structures, including not only the dorsal pallium-derived neocortex and medial pallium-derived hippocampal formation, but also the lateral pallium-derived claustrum–insular complex, and the ventral pallium-derived extended amygdaloid complex and olfactory centers.
evidence: This is a major finding of the study based on comprehensive labeling and imaging data presented throughout the results section.

claim: AACs are abundant in anterior olfactory nucleus, taenia tecta, and lateral septum.
source: AACs are also abundant in anterior olfactory nucleus, taenia tecta, and lateral septum.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: AACs show characteristic variations in density across neocortical areas and layers.
source: AACs show characteristic variations in density across neocortical areas and layers and across subregions of the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Neocortical AACs comprise multiple laminar subtypes with distinct dendritic and axonal arborization patterns.
source: Neocortical AACs comprise multiple laminar subtypes with distinct dendritic and axonal arborization patterns.
evidence: This is shown through single-cell morphological analysis in Figure 2g-j.

claim: The embryonic subpallium generates GABAergic neurons of the telencephalon.
source: The embryonic subpallium generates GABAergic neurons of the telencephalon, with the MGE giving rise to AACs (Kelly et al., 2019; Taniguchi et al., 2013) while other progenitor domains, such as the caudal ganglionic eminence (Miyoshi et al., 2015) or preoptic area (Gelman et al., 2011) do not.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: Within the MGE Nkx2.1 lineage, AACs are generated in two consecutive waves during both early and late neurogenesis.
source: Within the MGE Nkx2.1 lineage, AACs are generated in two consecutive waves during both early and late neurogenesis (Kelly et al., 2019), extending our initial report of their birth pattern (Taniguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a cited previous study by the authors.

claim: Late embryonic induction in the Nkx2.1CreER line only enriches a subset of neocortical AACs and also labels at least two other IN types.
source: Therefore, late embryonic induction in the Nkx2.1CreER line only enriches a subset of neocortical AACs and also labels at least two other IN types Kelly et al., 2019; this strategy also misses AACs in the hippocampus, BLA, and potentially other brain areas that are born earlier (Kelly et al., 2019).
evidence: This limitation is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: The Unc5bCreER line labels endothelial cells when combined with a reporter line.
source: Similarly, our Unc5bCreER line enabled adeno-associated virus (AAV) targeting of hippocampal AACs, but also labels endothelial cells when combined with a reporter line (Dudok et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the single driver line approach, based on a cited study.

claim: No singularly unique molecular marker for AACs has been identified.
source: Despite extensive effort to date, no singularly unique molecular marker for AACs has been identified.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the field.

claim: The same is true for most if not all neuronal subtypes of the mammalian brain (that no singularly unique molecular marker has been identified).
source: Indeed, the same is true for most if not all neuronal subtypes of the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in neuroscience.

claim: Postnatal high-dose TM induction generated dense and highly characteristic AAC labeling patterns throughout the neocortex, hippocampus, and BLA.
source: Indeed, postnatal high-dose TM induction generated dense and highly characteristic AAC labeling patterns throughout the neocortex, hippocampus, and BLA (Figure 1d–g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The characteristic chandelier axon arbor morphology with strings of synaptic boutons (cartridges) along the AIS of pyramidal neurons unequivocally indicated their AAC identity.
source: The characteristic chandelier axon arbor morphology with strings of synaptic boutons (cartridges) along the AIS of pyramidal neurons unequivocally indicated their AAC identity (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3), consistent with our previous high-resolution single-cell AAC imaging and reconstructions (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in figures and consistent with previous work.

claim: AACs and pAACs are abundantly present in essentially all pallium-derived structures and several additional structures.
source: Extensive analysis of these brain regions revealed an overarching pattern: AACs and pAACs are abundantly present in essentially all pallium-derived structures and several additional structures (Table 1; Figure 1c–g, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Video 1).
evidence: This is a major finding supported by comprehensive imaging data across multiple figures.

claim: The dPAL-derived structures include the entire neocortex and entorhinal/ectorhinal cortices.
source: The dPAL-derived structures include the entire neocortex and entorhinal/ectorhinal cortices.
evidence: This is stated as part of the comprehensive distribution pattern.

claim: The mPAL-derived structures include the entire hippocampal formation.
source: The mPAL-derived structures include the entire hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is stated as part of the comprehensive distribution pattern.

claim: pAACs are abundant in lPAL-derived claustrum, insular, and endopiriform dorsal.
source: Beyond these previously known structures, pAACs are abundant in lPAL-derived claustrum, insular, and endopiriform dorsal.
evidence: This is a novel finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The vPAL-derived structures include most of the amygdaloid complex (cortical amygdala, basolateral and basomedial amygdala, and medial amygdala) and extended amygdala (bed nucleus of stria terminalis).
source: In addition, the vPAL-derived structures include most of the amygdaloid complex (cortical amygdala, basolateral and basomedial amygdala, and medial amygdala) and extended amygdala (bed nucleus of stria terminalis).
evidence: This is stated as part of the comprehensive distribution pattern and shown in Figure 4.

claim: AACs are highly abundant in a set of olfactory centers including piriform cortex, AON, and TT.
source: Most surprisingly, AACs are highly abundant in a set of olfactory centers including piriform cortex, AON, and TT.
evidence: This is described as a surprising finding and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The piriform derives from the vPAL while AON and tenia tecta dorsal (TTd) derive from septum neuroepithelium.
source: Among these, the piriform derives from the vPAL while AON and tenia tecta dorsal (TTd) derive from septum neuroepithelium.
evidence: This is stated as developmental origin information.

claim: pAACs are found in lateral septum also derived from septum neuroepithelium.
source: Finally, pAACs are found in lateral septum also derived from septum neuroepithelium (Magno et al., 2022) and parts of the hypothalamus (derived largely from neuroepithelium of the third ventricle).
evidence: This is stated with a citation for the developmental origin.

claim: The PthlhFlp; Nkx2.1Cre; Ai65 mice were found to have an overall similar pattern of pAAC distribution across different brain regions, with several differences.
source: Consistent with these findings, the PthlhFlp; Nkx2.1Cre; Ai65 mice were found to have an overall similar pattern of pAAC distribution across different brain regions, with several differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between two intersectional strategies, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The Pthlh;Nkx2.1 intersection also labeled a set of layer 4 INs in the somatosensory cortex.
source: First, this intersection also labeled a set of layer 4 INs in the somatosensory cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This is stated as a difference between the two intersectional approaches.

claim: Pthlh;Nkx2.1 yielded slightly higher cell targeting in retrosplenial cortex.
source: Second, Pthlh;Nkx2.1 yielded slightly higher cell targeting in retrosplenial cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 3h, i).
evidence: This is stated as a difference between the two intersectional approaches.

claim: Pthlh;Nkx2.1 labeled fewer cells in the AON and BST.
source: Third, Pthlh;Nkx2.1 labeled fewer cells in the AON and BST.
evidence: This is stated as a difference between the two intersectional approaches.

claim: The PthlhFlp; Nkx2.1CreER; Ai65 mice led to exclusive fate mapping of AACs.
source: As an additional application of the PthlhFlp line, we demonstrate that when combined with an inducible Nkx2.1CreER driver (Taniguchi et al., 2013) the PthlhFlp; Nkx2.1CreER; Ai65 mice led to exclusive fate mapping of AACs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3j–l).
evidence: This is demonstrated in supplementary figures.

claim: The overall similarity between Unc5b/Nkx2.1 and Pthlh/Nkx2.1 patterns provided independent evidence that these intersectional approaches may have captured most if not all AACs in the brain.
source: The overall similarity between Unc5b/Nkx2.1 and Pthlh/Nkx2.1 patterns (except in layer 4 somatosensory cortex and striatum), and high density of cells captured, provided independent evidence that these intersectional approaches may have captured most if not all AACs in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of two independent methods.

claim: Intersection of PthlhFlp with the VipCre driver line was highly specific for an IN subtype with striking vertical morphology that may represent IN-selective cells.
source: First, consistent with its expression in a set of CGE-derived INs (including Vip-expressing cells), intersection with the VipCre driver line, which alone expresses in other cell types, was highly specific for an IN subtype with striking vertical morphology that may represent IN-selective cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3m-p).
evidence: This is demonstrated in supplementary figures.

claim: Pthlh/Nkx2.1 intersection yielded dense labeling of striatal INs.
source: Second, Pthlh/Nkx2.1 intersection yielded dense labeling of striatal INs (i.e. striatal neurons without axons in SNr/GPi) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f–h), consistent with known Pthlh expression in striatal Pvalb INs (Muñoz-Manchado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures and consistent with a cited study.

claim: The vast majority of RFP+ cells (97.3%, n = 110 cells from 6 mice) had axonal cartridge structure with synaptic boutons along PN AIS, validating their ChC identity.
source: Combined with immunolabeling of AnkyrinG-stained pyramidal neuron (PN) AIS, we showed that the vast majority of RFP+ cells (97.3%, n = 110 cells from 6 mice) had axonal cartridge structure with synaptic boutons along PN AIS, validating their ChC identity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: ChCs were detected across all areas of cerebral cortex.
source: ChCs were detected across all areas of cerebral cortex (Figure 2a; Video 1).
evidence: This is shown through whole-brain imaging and automated cell detection.

claim: The highest ChC densities were observed in ventrolateral areas such as PERI, ECT, TEA, and AI as well as ventromedially in infralimbic area (ILA).
source: The highest densities were observed in ventrolateral areas such as PERI, ECT, TEA, and AI as well as ventromedially in infralimbic area (ILA).
evidence: This is based on normalized cell density analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was a slight decline in ChC density very rostrally in FRP or caudally in RSP.
source: There was a slight decline in ChC density very rostrally in FRP or caudally in RSP.
evidence: This is based on normalized cell density analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The majority of ChC somas were located in L2/3, though this was area specific, with normalized density ranging from the lowest in SSs (65.5 ± 0.6%) to highest in VISp (94.7 ± 1.0%).
source: The majority of ChC somas were located in L2/3, though this was area specific, with normalized density ranging from the lowest in SSs (65.5 ± 0.6%) to highest in VISp (94.7 ± 1.0%).
evidence: This is based on quantitative laminar analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: ~80% of ChCs occupied a narrow band just below the L1/2 border.
source: An analysis of relative cortical depth (Figure 2e) revealed that ~80% of ChCs occupied a narrow band just below the L1/2 border, though this varied by anterior–posterior location.
evidence: This is based on cortical depth analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: ChCs were found at nearly all cortical depths, with a sizable proportion forming a second, less dense band above the white matter tract.
source: Nevertheless, ChCs were found at nearly all cortical depths, with a sizable proportion forming a second, less dense band above the white matter tract.
evidence: This is based on cortical depth analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Bi- and tri-laminar subtypes of ChCs were found rather frequently – L2/3 ChCs extending their axon arbors not only locally but further down to another one or two deep layers.
source: Notably, we found rather frequent bi- and tri-laminar subtypes – L2/3 ChCs extending their axon arbors not only locally but further down to another one or two deep layers (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is based on single-cell morphological analysis shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Translaminar ChCs may coordinate PN ensembles between cortical layers.
source: These translaminar ChCs may coordinate PN ensembles between cortical layers.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the morphological observation.

claim: The abundance of translaminar ChCs varied among cortical areas, for example with high abundance in auditory cortex.
source: The abundance of translaminar ChCs varied among cortical areas, for example with high abundance in auditory cortex (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is shown through morphological analysis in Figure 2j.

claim: ChC cartridges exhibited a wide range of densities across areas and layers.
source: ChC cartridges exhibited a wide range of densities across areas and layers (Figure 2m), with overall similarity to ChC soma densities in those areas and layers (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on cartridge density analysis shown in Figure 2m.

claim: The vast majority (98.2%, n = 56 cells, 6 mice) of labeled cells in hippocampus were AACs, characterized by vertically oriented cross laminar apical dendrites in CA1–CA3 and axon terminals innervating PN AIS.
source: Single-cell labeling by low-dose tamoxifen and immunohistochemistry confirmed that the vast majority (98.2%, n = 56 cells, 6 mice) were AACs, characterized by vertically oriented cross laminar apical dendrites in CA1–CA3 and axon terminals innervating PN AIS (Figure 3a, b, d).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: AAC density was highest in CA2 and lowest in dentate gyrus.
source: Dense labeling with high-dose TM followed by cell density analysis revealed that AAC density was, surprisingly, highest in CA2 and lowest in dentate gyrus (Figure 3c), with density in CA1 and CA3 approximately equal.
evidence: This is based on quantitative cell density analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Overall AAC density in CA2 was 3- to 4-fold greater than CA1/CA3 and 13-fold greater than dentate gyrus (DG).
source: Only a very sparse population of AAC was labeled in dentate gyrus. Overall AAC density in CA2 was 3- to 4-fold greater than CA1/CA3 and 13-fold greater than dentate gyrus (DG) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on quantitative cell density analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: This result suggests substantially different AAC–PN innervation ratio and that AACs may exert much denser and likely stronger control of CA2 PNs than CA1/CA3 PNs or DG granule cells.
source: As the density of PNs across hippocampal areas is overall similar, this result suggests substantially different AAC–PN innervation ratio and that AACs may exert much denser and likely stronger control of CA2 PNs than CA1/CA3 PNs or DG granule cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the density data and knowledge of PN distribution.

claim: The axon arbors of RFP cells in AI, CLA, EPd do not show clear laminar patterns and exhibit less uniformity and are more multipolar in morphology.
source: Unlike cortical and hippocampal AACs whose axon arbors exhibit highly characteristic laminar pattern, reflecting the organization of their postsynaptic targets (i.e. AIS of PNs), the axon arbors of RFP cells in AI, CLA, EPd do not show clear laminar patterns and exhibit less uniformity and are more multipolar in morphology (Figure 4b, c), making it more difficult to ascertain their identity.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Strings of synaptic boutons were frequently identified that co-localized with AnkG-labeled AIS, suggesting these as pAACs.
source: Nevertheless, strings of synaptic boutons were frequently identified that co-localized with AnkG-labeled AIS, suggesting these as pAACs.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry validation.

claim: Quantification from dense labeling revealed higher pAAC density in EPd compared to claustrum and EPv.
source: Quantification from dense labeling revealed higher pAAC density in EPd compared to claustrum and EPv, the latter of which structure is derived from vPAL (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on quantitative cell density analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: AACs or pAACs were found in all the amygdala nuclei containing GLU PNs, that is except CeA.
source: In this context, we found AACs or pAACs in all the amygdala nuclei containing GLU PNs, that is except CeA (Figure 4i–h).
evidence: This is based on comprehensive imaging across amygdala nuclei.

claim: Sparse labeling and immunohistochemical co-staining with AnkG confirmed that the labeled cells in amygdala compartments were nearly exclusively AIS-targeting (97.2%, n = 36 cells, 6 mice).
source: Sparse labeling and immunohistochemical co-staining with AnkG confirmed that the labeled cells in these compartments were nearly exclusively AIS-targeting (97.2%, n = 36 cells, 6 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: AACs in the amygdala tended to be similar to those in the claustrum, exhibiting multipolar dendrites and multipolar axon terminal branches.
source: Morphologically, AACs in the amygdala tended to be similar to those in the claustrum, exhibiting multipolar dendrites and multipolar axon terminal branches (in contrast to axon arbor of cortical AACs that typically extend either below or above the soma) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The density of AACs in amygdala appears to correlate with the known abundance of GLU PNs: densities in BLA, CoA, and BMA were much higher than those in MeA and BST.
source: The density of AACs in amygdala appears to correlate with the known abundance of GLU PNs: densities in BLA, CoA, and BMA were much higher than those in MeA and BST.
evidence: This is an inference based on density data and knowledge of PN distribution.

claim: AACs are deployed to all amygdala nuclei containing GLU PNs.
source: Our results indicate that AACs are deployed to all amygdala nuclei containing GLU PNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the distribution data.

claim: Within the largely GABAergic structures such as MeA and BST, pAACs might innervate the minor glutamatergic PNs in these structures.
source: Within the largely GABAergic structures such as MeA and BST, we hypothesize that pAACs might innervate the minor glutamatergic PNs in these structures.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the distribution pattern.

claim: The piriform cortex had been reported to contain axo-axonic synapses by co-localization of the inhibitory presynaptic marker GAT1 and AnkG.
source: Derived from the vPAL, the piriform cortex had been reported to contain axo-axonic synapses by co-localization of the inhibitory presynaptic marker GAT1 and AnkG (Wang and Sun, 2012).
evidence: This is based on a cited previous study.

claim: Dense labeling in Unc5bCreER; Nkx2.1Flp; Ai65 mice revealed a striking abundance of AACs that span the anterior-medial extent of the piriform in a single layer.
source: Our dense labeling in Unc5bCreER; Nkx2.1Flp; Ai65 mice revealed a striking abundance of AACs that span the anterior-medial extent of the piriform in a single layer (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sparse-labeled single AACs in piriform exhibited characteristic morphologies analogous to L2/3 AACs of the neocortex, with extended branching of apical dendrites to L1 and dense axon arbors below the cell body forming cartridges along PN AIS.
source: Sparse-labeled single AACs exhibited characteristic morphologies analogous to L2/3 AACs of the neocortex, with extended branching of apical dendrites to L1 and dense axon arbors below the cell body forming cartridges along PN AIS (Figure 5d–j).
evidence: This is based on single-cell morphological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The single-layer distribution pattern of piriform AACs continued dorsally to the insular cortex and ventrally to piriform-amygdala area (PAA) and COA.
source: The single-layer distribution pattern of piriform AACs continued dorsally to the insular cortex and ventrally to piriform-amygdala area (PAA) and COA (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: AACs in piriform, TT, and AON exhibited higher density than AACs in cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala.
source: Overall, AACs in piriform, TT, and AON exhibited higher density than AACs in cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala (Figure 6h, see Extended Data for Figures 2, 3, and 6).
evidence: This is based on quantitative density comparison shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Individual AACs in lateral septum were morphologically similar to cortical AACs, with extensive apical dendrites extending toward the midline and axon arbors and cartridges typically protruding away and into the cellular layer.
source: Individual AACs were morphologically similar to cortical AACs, with extensive apical dendrites extending toward the midline and axon arbors and cartridges typically protruding away and into the cellular layer (Figure 6i–k).
evidence: This is based on single-cell morphological analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: ChCsMOs received ~50% of inputs from motor areas (41.0 ± 2.3% in MOp, 4.5 ± 0.7% in contra MOs) followed by SSp (20.4 ± 4.2%) and SSs (9.5 ± 0.7%).
source: ChCsMOs received ~50% of inputs from motor areas (41.0 ± 2.3% in MOp, 4.5 ± 0.7% in contra MOs) followed by SSp (20.4 ± 4.2%) and SSs (9.5 ± 0.7%) (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Long-range inputs to ChCsMOp were largely dominated by sensory cortex (63.2 ± 11.3% in SSp, 10.1 ± 1.3% in SSs), followed by MOs (12.7 ± 6.7%) and contra MOp (4.2 ± 2.5%).
source: Long-range inputs to ChCsMOp were largely dominated by sensory cortex (63.2 ± 11.3% in SSp, 10.1 ± 1.3% in SSs), followed by MOs (12.7 ± 6.7%) and contra MOp (4.2 ± 2.5%) (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: ChCsSSp received only ~65% inputs total from sensorimotor (42.2 ± 0.5% in SSs, 11.1 ± 1.2% in MOs, 7.8 ± 1.9% in MOp, 3.03 ± 0.2% in contra SSp), with considerably more inputs from thalamus and other cortical areas.
source: In contrast, ChCsSSp received only ~65% inputs total from sensorimotor (42.2 ± 0.5% in SSs, 11.1 ± 1.2% in MOs, 7.8 ± 1.9% in MOp, 3.03 ± 0.2% in contra SSp), with considerably more inputs from thalamus and other cortical areas (Figure 7g).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Thalamocortical (TC) afferents to ChCsMOs and ChCsMOp were primarily from VAL, whereas TC inputs to ChCsSSp were mostly from ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM).
source: Thalamocortical (TC) afferents to ChCsMOs and ChCsMOp were primarily from VAL, whereas TC inputs to ChCsSSp were mostly from ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM).
evidence: This is based on input tracing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sparse inputs from GPe directly to ChCs and Pvalb were identified in all three cortical areas.
source: Interestingly, we identified sparse inputs from GPe directly to ChCs and Pvalb in all three cortical areas.
evidence: This is based on input tracing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Overall input patterns were comparable between ChCs and Pvalb, although ChCs received significantly less homotypic inputs from the contralateral hemisphere for each injection site.
source: Overall input patterns were comparable between ChCs and Pvalb, although ChCs received significantly less homotypic inputs from the contralateral hemisphere for each injection site (Figure 7e–g).
evidence: This is based on comparative input tracing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: AACsCA1 received asymmetric inputs from each hemisphere, with relatively a higher fraction in CA3 contralaterally (29.0 ± 2.4%) but higher ipsilaterally in DG (4.3 ± 1.5%) and ENT (11.6 ± 3.6%) and SUB (15.2 ± 5.2%).
source: Within the hippocampus formation, AACsCA1 received asymmetric inputs from each hemisphere, with relatively a higher fraction in CA3 contralaterally (29.0 ± 2.4%) but higher ipsilaterally in DG (4.3 ± 1.5%) and ENT (11.6 ± 3.6%) and SUB (15.2 ± 5.2%) (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: In AACsCA1 over twofold higher input connectivity was found from adjacent NDB (5.1 ± 0.9%) compared to MS (2.0 ± 0.2%).
source: Surprisingly, while the aforementioned study Viney et al., 2013 found inhibitory connections from MS to AACs in CA3, we found in AACsCA1 over twofold higher input connectivity from adjacent NDB (5.1 ± 0.9%) compared to MS (2.0 ± 0.2%) (Figure 8d, e).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The majority of long-range inputs to AACsCA1 from MS/NDB were inhibitory (56.8 ± 4.8%) and a sizeable proportion ChAT-positive (27.6 ± 4.0%).
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis found the majority of these long-range inputs were inhibitory (56.8 ± 4.8%) and a sizeable proportion ChAT-positive (27.6 ± 4.0%) (Figure 8f–j).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry marker analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: AACsBLA received strongest afferents from PIR (13.1 ± 1.1%) and the hippocampal–entorhinal network (ENT 12.7 ± 0.2%, CA1 10.5 ± 2.0%, SUB 8.0 ± 0.1%).
source: AACsBLA received strongest afferents from PIR (13.1 ± 1.1%) and the hippocampal–entorhinal network (ENT 12.7 ± 0.2%, CA1 10.5 ± 2.0%, SUB 8.0 ± 0.1%) (Figure 9e, h–i).
evidence: This is based on quantitative input tracing data shown in Figure 9.

claim: TC afferents to AACsBLA were largely from MTN (2.6 ± 0.4%).
source: TC afferents were largely from MTN (2.6 ± 0.4%), while cortical projections were identified in AI, AUD, PERI, and ECT (Figure 9f).
evidence: This is based on input tracing data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Input cells to AACsBLA in LZ and MEZ of hypothalamus were found to be glutamatergic, while those from GPe and EP were GABAergic.
source: Input cells in LZ and MEZ of hypothalamus were found to be glutamatergic, while those from GPe and EP were GABAergic (Figure 9j–o).
evidence: This is based on marker analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: AACs may exert decisive control over spike generation in ensembles of PNs, thereby regulating network operations and information relay.
source: Because AIS are the site of action potential initiation and individual AACs innervate hundreds of PNs in their vicinity, AACs are thought to exert decisive control over spike generation in ensembles of PNs (Crick et al., 1986; Howard et al., 2005), thereby regulating network operations and information relay.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on cited previous work.

claim: The Vipr2-Cre driver captures a subset of neocortical and basolateral amygdala (BLA) AACs, but is not entirely specific in these areas.
source: For example, the Vipr2-Cre driver captures a subset of neocortical and basolateral amygdala (BLA) AACs, but is not entirely specific in these areas (Daigle et al., 2018; Nakashima et al., 2022; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The MeA and BST comprise mostly GABAergic neurons that are primarily generated from the subpallium.
source: Notably, although the MeA and BST comprise mostly GABAergic neurons that are primarily generated from the subpallium, they contain subsets of glutamatergic PN that migrate from pallium origin (Beyeler and Dabrowska, 2020) or from the third ventricle (García-Moreno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The pallium may have its evolutionary origin in an anterior region of the vertebrate hypothalamus.
source: In this context, it is notable that the pallium may have its evolutionary origin in an anterior region of the vertebrate hypothalamus (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited previous study.

claim: The number and density of GABAergic synapses at AIS vary substantially among different PyNs within and across cortical layers.
source: Consistent with these results, the number and density of GABAergic synapses at AIS also vary substantially among different PyNs within and across cortical layers (DeFelipe et al., 1985; Fish et al., 2013; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on cited previous studies.

claim: The simpler circuit architecture and strong link to innate rodent behaviors of olfactory centers may facilitate uncovering the logic of AAC function.
source: Although the functional significance is not yet clear, the simpler circuit architecture and strong link to innate rodent behaviors of these olfactory centers may facilitate uncovering the logic of AAC function.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Olfactory circuits are evolutionarily preserved across vertebrate species.
source: Furthermore, as these olfactory circuits are evolutionarily preserved across vertebrate species (Zeppilli et al., 2023), our finding raises the possibility that AACs might be present in the CNS of other vertebrates, beyond the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is stated based on a cited study and leads to a speculation.
